summary: The reviewed code file (**`aeropulse_space_mission_avatar_simulator.html`**) is a comprehensive, web-based **Space Mission Design and Operations Simulator** designed for hackathons like the **NASA Space Apps Challenge**, running entirely within a single HTML file. The platform enables users to select interplanetary mission objectives, configure spacecraft architectures by balancing engineering constraints such as budget, mass, and power across launch vehicles, power sources, scientific payloads, and communications systems. It features an interactive **Pilot Avatar and Suit Armory** system where players can choose pilot classes (Science Astronaut or Space Warrior) and upgrade modules like helmets, armor, jetpacks, and nano-tools. During real-time flight simulations covering atmospheric ascent, trajectory correction, and orbital insertion, users must manage critical anomalies like solar flares and micrometeoroid impacts using their pilot armor and backup subsystems. Finally, the mission concludes with a detailed **Debrief Report** evaluating system reliability, budget efficiency, and collected science points to generate a comprehensive grade and engineering lessons learned, all styled within a modern, dark-mode aerospace mission control interface powered by Tailwind CSS, FontAwesome, and JavaScript.
details: The AeroPulse project, developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, is an interactive, web-based space mission design and operations simulator that runs entirely within a single HTML file. The platform allows users to conceptualize interplanetary missions by balancing complex engineering constraints such as budget limits, mass capacities, and power margins across launch vehicles, power sources, scientific payloads, and communications systems. It features an advanced Pilot Avatar and Suit Armory system where players can choose between a Science Astronaut or Space Warrior class and upgrade modules like helmets, armor, jetpacks, and nano-tools using gear credits. During real-time flight simulations covering atmospheric ascent, trajectory correction, orbital insertion, and scientific operations, users must navigate critical anomalies like solar radiation storms and micrometeoroid impacts by leveraging their pilot armor and backup subsystems. Finally, the mission concludes with a comprehensive Debrief Report that evaluates system reliability, budget efficiency, and collected science points to generate a final grade, hardware manifest breakdown, and engineering lessons learned, all styled within a dark-mode aerospace mission control interface powered by Tailwind CSS, FontAwesome, and modern JavaScript.
